Render unto Caesar
REN-der UN-too SEE-zer
noun phrase (Matthew 22:21)
From the Lord's word, “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Matthew 22:21); the principle of the distinct claims of the civil power and of God.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

📖 Biblical Definition

“Render unto Caesar” is the principle, grounded in the Lord's famous answer, of the distinct and ordered claims of the civil power and of God. When the Pharisees and Herodians sought to trap Him over the tribute money, Jesus called for a coin, asked whose image and superscription it bore, and answered, “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.” The saying establishes that the civil magistrate has a real and God-given claim—taxes, tribute, honour, lawful obedience—which the believer is bound to render, as Paul confirms: “Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due… honour to whom honour.” Yet it equally establishes the limit of Caesar's claim: the things that are God's are not Caesar's. The coin bears Caesar's image and may be rendered to him; but man bears the image of God, and the worship, faith, and conscience of man belong to God alone, never to the state. The dictionary marks the doctrine against two errors. The first is the statism that lets Caesar claim what is God's—demanding the conscience, the worship, the ultimate allegiance that belong to God—against which the apostles answered, “We ought to obey God rather than men.” The second is the anarchic or sectarian spirit that withholds from Caesar even his lawful due—refusing taxes, honour, and ordinary obedience under a false claim of Christian liberty. The dictionary holds the Lord's balance: honour the king and pay the tribute that is Caesar's, but render to God the worship and obedience that are His alone, and when Caesar demands what is God's, obey God rather than men.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Lord's principle of the distinct claims of the state and of God (Matthew 22:21): render Caesar his lawful due—tribute, honour, obedience—but render to God the worship and conscience that are His alone, never the state's.

RENDER UNTO CAESAR, noun phrase. The principle of the distinct claims of the civil power and of God.

“Render unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Matthew 22:21).

Caesar's due: tribute, custom, fear, honour, lawful obedience (Romans 13:7).

God's due: worship, faith, and conscience, which Caesar may not claim.

When Caesar demands what is God's: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

📖 Key Scripture

Mt 22:21 — "They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's."

Ro 13:7 — "Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour."

Ac 5:29 — "Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men."

1 Pe 2:17 — "Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Statism lets Caesar claim what is God's—the conscience, the worship, ultimate allegiance; the anarchic spirit withholds from Caesar even his lawful due of tribute, honour, and obedience.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ordered distinction of the two claims. The first corruption is statism: letting Caesar claim the things that are God's. The coin bears Caesar's image and may be rendered to him; but man bears the image of God, and his worship, faith, and conscience belong to God alone. When the state demands the ultimate allegiance, the bowed conscience, or the worship due to God—as Caesars ancient and modern have—the believer must answer with the apostles, “We ought to obey God rather than men.” The state that claims what is God's has overstepped the bound the Lord Himself set.

The opposite corruption is the anarchic or sectarian spirit that withholds from Caesar even his lawful due—refusing taxes, honour, and ordinary obedience under a false banner of Christian liberty. But the Lord commanded the tribute rendered, and Paul confirms it: render to all their dues, tribute and custom and honour. The dictionary holds the Lord's balance exactly: honour the king and pay what is Caesar's, render to God the worship and obedience that are His alone, and when the two claims collide—when Caesar demands what belongs to God—obey God rather than men, and bear the cost.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Lord's saying on the tribute money (Matthew 22:21); “Caesar” the title of the Roman emperor, here the civil power, whose “image and superscription” the coin bore.

expand to see more

“Render” (Greek apodidomi, to give back what is owed).

“Caesar,” the title of the Roman emperor, here the civil power.

The coin bore Caesar's “image and superscription” (Matthew 22:20).

Man bears the image of God; his worship and conscience are God's.

The bound on Caesar: he may not claim the things that are God's.

Usage

"The pastor preached “render unto Caesar” to bound the state: it may not claim the conscience."

"He taught the believer to pay tribute and honour the king, withholding only what is God's."

"She obeyed God rather than men when Caesar demanded the worship due to God alone."
